messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing a psychological case vignette
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

Write a realistic clinical case vignette for a patient with PTSD.
The vignette should read as a cohesive, flowing portrait — not a structured report.
Weave together who this person is, what happened to them, how they experience their
symptoms day to day, how they cope, and what toll this takes on their life and relationships.


Do not use section headers, numbered points, or clinical labels for symptoms.
Write 200–300 words in third person.
Cover: presenting complaints, trauma background, cognitive distortions, avoidance, and maintaining factors.
Avoid excessive jargon - write for a clinical case conference audience.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient presenting with PTSD.
Patient demographics:
- Age: 60
- Gender: Female
- Ethnicity: European
- Relationship Status: In a relationship
- Occupation: Midwife
- Trauma Type: Toxic chemical exposure
- Pcl5: 54

She is 60, European, and has worked as a midwife for most of her adult life. She speaks about birth with the kind of reverence that makes it sound almost sacred: the rhythm of labor, the instinctive quiet in a delivery room when a baby crowns, the small, competent tasks that steady frightened mothers. For years she has been known as the one who remains calm when others panic. She says she never imagined that what would undo her sense of safety would not be blood or emergency, but a smell.

The exposure happens on an ordinary shift. A disinfecting agent has recently been changed on her unit, and that morning there is already some grumbling among staff about the sharpness of it. She notices the odor as soon as she enters a patient room—strong, metallic, almost sweet in a way that makes the back of her throat tighten. At first she keeps working. She adjusts monitors, reassures a laboring woman, and tells herself it is unpleasant but harmless. Within minutes, though, her eyes begin to sting. She feels lightheaded, then strangely detached, as if the room has slid half a step away from her. Her chest tightens. Someone says her name twice before she answers. She remembers gripping the bedrail because she is suddenly afraid she might faint onto the floor in front of the patient.

There is confusion after that. A coworker opens windows. Another staff member starts coughing. She is helped into the corridor, where the air feels no better. She can still recall the smell clinging to her uniform, to her hair, to the inside of her nose. She feels nauseated and unsteady, humiliated by how little control she has over her own body. At the hospital clinic she is told she has likely had a toxic exposure. People are efficient and reassuring, but she hears only fragments. What lodges in her mind is the primitive certainty that something invisible has entered her body and may keep harming her long after she leaves the building.

In the weeks afterward, she expects to recover quickly. Instead, the world becomes organized around threat. The smell returns in memory with astonishing force. Walking past cleaning supplies in a supermarket, she is suddenly back in that patient room, throat closing, heart pounding. If a neighbor uses bleach, she shuts all the windows and paces from room to room, furious and frightened at once. She begins washing her work clothes separately, then asks her partner to leave shoes outside. She checks labels obsessively, scanning for ingredients she does not understand. She knows some of this sounds excessive, but the fear arrives faster than reason.

Returning to work is especially painful. She still loves midwifery, still feels drawn to women in labor, but now every odor in the hospital feels loaded. Hand sanitizer, floor cleaner, adhesive remover—each one makes her body brace before her mind has caught up. She notices exits in every room. During deliveries she positions herself near the door. She starts volunteering for tasks she can do away from recently cleaned spaces, then feels ashamed, as though she is no longer the dependable colleague she once was. On the drive in, her stomach clenches so tightly she sometimes has to pull over. She has begun dreading the place where she spent decades feeling useful and at home.

At night, the event replays not as a clear film but in fragments: the burning in her eyes, the chemical sweetness, the sudden conviction that she is about to collapse. She wakes with her heart racing and sits upright, trying to smell the air in the bedroom. Her partner reaches for her, but she is often already out of bed, checking windows, checking the radiator, trying to identify some source of contamination that is not there. She has become irritable in ways that surprise her. Small things—air freshener in a taxi, detergent on someone’s coat, a scented candle at a friend’s house—can leave her tense for hours. She avoids restaurants, hotels, and other people’s homes because she cannot control what products have been used there.

What troubles her most is the narrowing of her life. She used to be sociable, practical, amused by fuss. Now she plans routes based on which shops smell “safe.” She sits near open windows even in cold weather. She no longer lingers after shifts to chat with younger midwives. When mothers thank her, she smiles, but she is often fighting the urge to get out of the room and into fresh air. She says she feels as if her body has become a faulty alarm system, sounding danger everywhere.

Even now, months later, she speaks about the exposure with a mixture of anger and disbelief. She cannot understand why one incident continues to live inside her so vividly. Part of her knows she survived it; another part still behaves as though the threat is present and airborne. She misses the version of herself who could enter any room and think first of the person needing care, not of what she might be breathing.
